title: Balancing Public Transport Investment and Road Maintenance
essay:
In recent debates surrounding urban planning, an increasingly prominent view is that public funding should be redirected predominantly toward mass transit systems rather than highway construction. While I strongly advocate for prioritizing investments in public transit to foster sustainable communities, I believe governments must still allocate sufficient capital to preserve vital road infrastructure.

Directing the majority of state expenditure into expanding train networks, subway lines, and bus routes provides immense socioeconomic and environmental advantages. Primary among these is affordability for commuters. Rising fuel prices and vehicle maintenance make private motoring economically prohibitive for many households. Reliable transit options therefore provide a cost-effective alternative, enabling lower-income residents to gain dependable access to jobs, education, and essential public services across sprawling metropolitan areas. Furthermore, high-capacity transport is the most practical remedy for traffic gridlock. When workers have access to efficient, modern train or bus rapid transit corridors, large numbers of private cars are removed from city thoroughfares, leading to lower congestion and reduced carbon emissions.

Nevertheless, this prioritization should not come at the expense of abandoning roadways, as doing so would cause severe regional disparities. Highway systems are essential for freight logistics and the movement of goods that drive national economies. More crucially, authorities have a duty to protect rural connections. In remote country towns and sparsely populated agricultural districts, building extensive mass transit systems such as light rail is rarely economically viable or logistically feasible. Inhabitants in these outlying regions depend heavily on private vehicles and local road networks to commute, visit hospitals, and access central marketplaces. Neglecting road preservation would inevitably isolate these communities and stifle local economic activity.

In conclusion, I largely agree that public transport should receive the lion's share of transport budgets due to its affordability, employment connectivity, and power to relieve congestion. However, balanced fiscal planning demands that essential roads are properly maintained to ensure regional equality.

requirements.prompt: Some people think governments should spend more on public transport than on roads. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
requirements.position: Prioritize public transport while maintaining essential roads.
requirements.ideas: Affordability for commuters; access to jobs; lower congestion; protect rural connections.

requirement_notes: Position: Prioritize public transport while maintaining essential roads is explicitly stated in the thesis statement and reaffirmed in the conclusion.
Idea 'Affordability for commuters': Developed in Body Paragraph 1 as a key benefit of transit over private car ownership.
Idea 'Access to jobs': Elaborated in Body Paragraph 1 regarding connecting lower-income workers to employment opportunities across metropolitan areas.
Idea 'Lower congestion': Developed in Body Paragraph 1 by explaining how high-capacity transit takes cars off the roads to ease gridlock.
Idea 'Protect rural connections': Fully integrated into Body Paragraph 2 to explain why road maintenance must not be abandoned, particularly for remote populations lacking transit infrastructure.

IELTS academic_task_2 | Coherence and Cohesion | criterion_definition
This criterion is concerned with the overall organisation and logical development of 
the message: how the response organises and links information, ideas and language. 
Coherence refers to the linking of ideas through logical sequencing, while cohesion 
refers to the varied and appropriate use of cohesive devices (e.g. logical connectors, 
conjunctions and pronouns) to assist in making clear the relationships between and 
within sentences. 
 
The CC criterion assesses: 
 
▪ the coherence of the response via the logical organisation of information 
and/or ideas, or the logical progression of the argument. 
▪ the appropriate use of paragraphing for topic organisation and presentation. 
▪ the logical sequencing of ideas and/or information within and across 
paragraphs. 
▪ the flexible use of reference and substitution (e.g. definite articles, pronouns). 
▪ the appropriate use of discourse markers to clearly mark the stages in a 
response, e.g. [First of all | In conclusion], and to signal the relationship between 
ideas and/or information, e.g. [as a result | similarly].
